lead: Every optical receiver guesses each bit. Noise makes the sampled current wander, so a 1 can fall below the decision threshold or a 0 can rise above it. The bit error rate (BER) is the probability of a wrong guess. One number, the Q factor, measures how far apart the two levels are compared with their noise, and Q alone fixes the BER. The eye diagram shows the same thing on an oscilloscope, and the power penalty says how much extra light a degraded receiver needs to get back to the target BER. Only a few universities teach this as a topic of its own.
prereq: You need the noise currents of Photodetector noise and the receiver chain of Optical receiver structure and sensitivity.

sections.h3: Signal, noise and one number Q

blocks.text: At the sampling instant the receiver holds a current. For a 1 bit its mean is I<sub>1</sub>, for a 0 bit I<sub>0</sub>, and the rms noise on each is σ<sub>1</sub> and σ<sub>0</sub>, all in amperes. Noise is taken as Gaussian. The decision threshold I<sub>D</sub> lies between the levels: a sample above I<sub>D</sub> is called 1, below it 0.

Errors happen in two ways: a 1 whose sample falls below I<sub>D</sub>, and a 0 whose sample rises above it. The 1 level is (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>)/σ<sub>1</sub> standard deviations above the threshold, and the 0 level is (I<sub>D</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/σ<sub>0</sub> below it. The best threshold makes these two numbers equal; that common value is Q.
Q has no units. It is the gap between the levels measured in units of the sum of the two noises.

This is the best threshold (very nearly exact for Gaussian noise). With σ<sub>1</sub> = σ<sub>0</sub> it is halfway between the levels. When the 1 level is noisier (shot noise, APD noise), the threshold moves down towards the quieter 0 level.

sections.h3: BER from Q, and the eye diagram

blocks.text: With equally likely ones and zeros and the best threshold, each error type has probability ½erfc(Q/√2), and the BER is
erfc is the complementary error function. The approximation is within about 10 % for Q above 3 and within 3 % for Q ≥ 6.

So Q = 6 gives BER ≈ 10⁻⁹ and Q ≈ 7 gives 10⁻¹². Each extra unit of Q buys roughly two to three decades of BER. Multiply BER by the bit rate to get errors per second: at 10 Gbit/s, BER = 10⁻⁹ is about 10 errors every second.

The eye diagram overlays many bit periods on an oscilloscope. At the sampling instant its vertical opening is the gap I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>; the margins Qσ<sub>1</sub> below the 1 level and Qσ<sub>0</sub> above the 0 level must fit inside that gap. Noise thickens the traces; intersymbol interference from dispersion or a slow receiver pulls the levels towards each other; timing jitter moves the sampling point sideways. All three close the eye and raise the BER.
To compare receivers, ask how much more optical power brings the BER back to the target. The power penalty is
P<sub>1</sub> is the average power needed before the change and P<sub>2</sub> after it, in the same unit.

If the noise does not depend on the signal (thermal noise), Q is proportional to P, so the penalty for moving from Q<sub>1</sub> to Q<sub>2</sub> is 10 log₁₀(Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>). If shot noise dominates, σ ∝ √P, so Q ∝ √P and the penalty is 20 log₁₀(Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>). Always state the noise regime.

A finite extinction ratio r<sub>ex</sub> = P<sub>0</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> (light left in the zero) shrinks the gap for the same average power. With thermal noise the penalty is 10 log₁₀[(1 + r<sub>ex</sub>)/(1 − r<sub>ex</sub>)]: 0.87 dB for r<sub>ex</sub> = 0.1. A BER floor is different: the curve of BER against power flattens and more power stops helping. It comes from disturbances that do not shrink as the signal grows, such as interference, mode-partition noise, modal noise and pattern-dependent jitter. APD excess noise does not cause a floor: it enlarges σ<sub>1</sub> and σ<sub>0</sub> and moves the threshold, but more power still lowers the BER. Dispersion and jitter penalties of whole links are part of link design (the power and rise-time budgets).

examples.question: A receiver has I<sub>1</sub> = 1.0 µA and I<sub>0</sub> = 0.10 µA. (a) With thermal noise σ<sub>1</sub> = σ<sub>0</sub> = 0.075 µA, find Q, the best threshold and the BER. (b) With signal-dependent noise σ<sub>1</sub> = 0.10 µA and σ<sub>0</sub> = 0.05 µA, find Q and the best threshold, and the BER if the threshold were left halfway. (c) The target is changed to 10⁻¹². Find the power penalty from case (a) for fixed noise and for shot-limited noise.
steps: (a) Equal noise, so I<sub>D</sub> is halfway: (1.0 + 0.10)/2 = 0.55 µA. BER = ½erfc(6/√2) = 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁰, about 10⁻⁹.

(b) Threshold left at 0.55 µA: the 1 level is only (1.0 − 0.55)/0.10 = 4.5σ<sub>1</sub> away, the 0 level (0.55 − 0.10)/0.05 = 9σ<sub>0</sub>. BER = ½[½erfc(4.5/√2) + ½erfc(9/√2)] = ½ × 3.4 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶, about 1700 times worse.
(c) Fixed (thermal) noise: Q ∝ P, so P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = 7.03/6.0 = 1.172 and the penalty is 10 log₁₀ 1.172 = 0.69 dB.
(c) Shot-limited noise: Q ∝ √P, so P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = (7.03/6.0)² = 1.374 and the penalty is 10 log₁₀ 1.374 = 1.38 dB.
examples.answer: (a) Q = 6.0, I<sub>D</sub> = 0.55 µA, BER ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁹. (b) Q = 6.0 with I<sub>D</sub> = 0.40 µA; a halfway threshold would give 1.7 × 10⁻⁶. (c) Q<sub>2</sub> = 7.03; penalty 0.69 dB with fixed noise, 1.38 dB when shot-limited.

traps: Using only σ<sub>1</sub> or only σ<sub>0</sub> in Q. Q uses σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>.
Leaving the threshold halfway when the noises differ. In the example that turns 10⁻⁹ into 1.7 × 10⁻⁶.
Using 20 log₁₀(Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>) for fixed noise. Fixed (thermal) noise gives 10 log₁₀; shot-limited noise gives 20 log₁₀.
Blaming a BER floor on APD excess noise. A floor needs a disturbance that does not fall as the signal grows; excess noise only steepens the power needed.
Putting the extinction ratio in dB into (1 + r<sub>ex</sub>)/(1 − r<sub>ex</sub>). Use the linear ratio r<sub>ex</sub> = P<sub>0</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>.

quiz.q: Define Q for a receiver with mean levels I<sub>1</sub>, I<sub>0</sub> and rms noises σ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>0</sub>.
quiz.a: Q = (I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>0</sub>), with no units.

quiz.q: Why is the best decision threshold not always halfway between I<sub>1</sub> and I<sub>0</sub>?
quiz.a: The best threshold makes both levels the same number of their own standard deviations away. When σ<sub>1</sub> > σ<sub>0</sub> that point is closer to I<sub>0</sub>: I<sub>D</sub> = (σ<sub>0</sub>I<sub>1</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>I<sub>0</sub>)/(σ<sub>0</sub> + σ<sub>1</sub>).

quiz.q: I<sub>1</sub> = 1.2 µA, I<sub>0</sub> = 0.1 µA, σ<sub>1</sub> = σ<sub>0</sub> = 0.1 µA. Find Q and the BER.
At low power the BER of a receiver falls as expected, but above some power it stays at 10⁻¹⁰ however much light is added. What does that tell you?
quiz.a: There is a BER floor: an error source that does not shrink as the signal grows, such as interference, mode-partition noise or pattern-dependent jitter. More power will not help; that impairment must be removed.

quiz.q: Write the large-Q approximation of the BER.
quiz.a: BER ≈ e<sup>−Q²/2</sup>/(Q√(2π)), good for Q above about 3.

quiz.q: A fixed-noise power penalty is 2 dB. By what factor must Q increase?
quiz.a: With fixed noise Q ∝ P, so Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub> = 10<sup>2/10</sup> = 1.585.

quiz.q: Find the extinction-ratio penalty for r<sub>ex</sub> = 0.05 in a thermal-noise-limited receiver.

beyond: Not for the exam. Forward error correction lets a link run at a raw BER near 10⁻³ and still deliver 10⁻¹² or better after decoding, so the Q needed before decoding drops sharply. Coherent receivers use multilevel formats and soft decisions, where Q is an intermediate measure rather than the final one. BER testers send pseudo-random bit sequences and count errors; Q is also estimated from eye measurements when errors are too rare to count. Search next for "BER tester", "forward error correction threshold" and "Q factor from eye diagram".

figure.caption: Top: case (b) of the worked example. The 1 level is twice as noisy as the 0 level, so the best threshold, 0.40 µA, sits six noise widths from each level; leaving it halfway at 0.55 µA raises the BER from 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ to 1.7 × 10⁻⁶. Bottom: BER against Q; Q = 6 gives about 10⁻⁹ and Q = 7.03 gives 10⁻¹².

spec.aria: Top: two bell curves of sampled current, a narrow one at 0.10 microamperes and a wider one at 1.0 microamperes, with a solid threshold at 0.40 and a dashed one at 0.55. Bottom: bit error rate on a log scale from 10 to the minus 1 to 10 to the minus 16 against Q from 2 to 8, falling steeply, with points at Q equals 6 and Q equals 7.03.
